**A language model is just another channel.** Call it from a process, synchronously or asynchronously, and stream the answer to the waiting caller.

**2026-10-24.** A process can call a language model — synchronously or asynchronously — and
stream the answer to its caller.

There is no new BPMN element. A model call is an ordinary **channel call**, so it gets everything a
channel call already has: `<q:timeout>`, `<q:retry>`, timer and error boundaries, correlation. One
attribute joins the `q:` vocabulary, additively: `q:stream`.

## Sync or async: the outbound channel says which

| Outbound `ack-mode` | Pattern | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `on-complete` | **sync** | The call is made inline and its answer merged into the variables; the flow carries on. No park, no outbox row, no database write for the hop. Parallel branches' calls are in flight together. |
| `on-persist` (default) | **async** | The request goes through the outbox, the flow parks, and the answer arrives on an inbound channel and resumes it by correlation. |

Sync works wherever a pass is driven — a start, a relayed turn, a timer, a scheduled start — and an
HTTP caller gets the flow's reply on its own request, turn after turn. Sync REST calls use the same
mechanism (`transport: http`).

## How it looks

```xml
<bpmn:serviceTask id="Summarize" implementation="channel:summarize">
  <bpmn:extensionElements>
    <q:alias name="ticket" expression="body.request.ticketId"/>
  </bpmn:extensionElements>
</bpmn:serviceTask>
```

```yaml
channels:
  - name: summarize
    direction: outbound
    transport: llm
    bind: "llm://summarize"
    llm:
      reply-channel: summarize-reply
      candidates:
        - { provider: anthropic, model: <model-id>, api-key: "secret:llm/anthropic" }
        - { provider: mistral,   model: <model-id>, api-key: "env:MISTRAL_KEY" }
  - name: summarize-reply
    transport: local
    codec: json
```

The task's input is `{ "prompt": "…" }` (or a `messages` conversation, `tools`, `json: true`, …);
the answer arrives on `summarize-reply` with `text`, `toolCalls`, `finish`, `usage`, the model that
answered, and the request echoed for correlation. The full reference is
Calling a language model in the book (`building/llm-channels.md`).

## Providers

`openai`, `anthropic`, `aws-bedrock`, `google-gemini`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `xai`, `kimi`,
`meta-llama`. Most speak the Chat Completions wire format and share one adapter;
the `provider:` id picks the default endpoint, and `base-url` overrides it for a regional host,
a proxy or a self-hosted server.

Candidates are tried in order. A rate limit, an outage or a timeout moves on to the next one; a
rejected request or a filtered answer does not — the first cannot be fixed by asking someone else,
and the second is an answer.

## Jobs, webhooks and streaming

- **Jobs** (`llm.mode: job`): the provider holds the work. Sutra submits, returns at once, and
  completes by polling or by a **signed webhook**; the flow sees the same reply either way.
- **Streaming** (`reply-stream: sse` on the inbound channel, `q:stream="true"` on the task): the
  caller receives the answer as server-sent events while it is generated; the flow still sees the
  whole answer. Chunks are never logged.

## What the engine learned

Nothing about models. It gained three neutral hooks — `InlineCaller` (a transport that answers a
call synchronously), `ReplySinkFactory` (a sink that answers by re-entering the engine) and a
streaming variant of the inline call — and a crash-recovery marker for in-memory chains. Provider
adapters plug into the `llm` transport through `sutra-llm-spi`, which names no provider.

## Behaviour changes

A plain `<q:reply>` that a flow reaches before it parks now answers the request — for a start and
for each relayed turn. Previously only `<q:reply continue="true">` did, and a start that replied
then parked returned `200` with an empty body.

A structured request or send body — a channel-call `requestBody`, a `<q:send>`, a
destination-bearing `<q:reply>` — is now sent as JSON instead of FEEL's canonical text (`{a=1}`),
which no counterpart could parse. String bodies are unchanged.

## Examples, and what CI covers

Two example packages: `examples/ai-summarize` (sync, streamed and async summaries) and
`examples/ai-advanced` (cross-provider fallback, JSON mode, a tool call, OpenAI background jobs
polled and webhook-completed, an Anthropic Message Batch). Each keeps its flows once under
`shared/` and one `channels.yaml` per provider under `variants/`, composed with the existing
overlay mechanism:

```bash
sutra package examples/ai-summarize/variants/anthropic --overlay examples/ai-summarize/shared \
    --out examples/ai-summarize/deploy/deployments
```

**In CI (tier 2, no keys):** the stub variants, composed through that overlay path, run on a real
engine and PostgreSQL against a stub model server that speaks the OpenAI and Anthropic wire
formats — sync, SSE-streamed and async calls over both wires; cross-provider fallback, Anthropic
down then up; JSON mode; a tool call; an OpenAI background job, polled; one completed by a signed
webhook; an Anthropic Message Batch. The tests check the replies, the streamed frames, the sink
deliveries and the engine's `instance_state` and `llm_job` rows. Every variant, the real-provider
ones included, is linted in tier 1.

**Against the real providers:** `examples/ai-advanced/live-check.sh` runs both examples with your
keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini; the webhook needs a tunnel and `OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET`).

## Verified against real providers

The `examples/ai-summarize` flows — sync, streamed and async — ran end to end against OpenAI
(`gpt-4o-mini`), Anthropic (`claude-haiku-5-5`) and Google Gemini (`gemini-2.5-flash`). Against
OpenAI, candidate fallback (an unreachable first candidate, then OpenAI), JSON mode, tool calls and
an OpenAI background job — completed both by polling and by a signed webhook through a public
tunnel — passed too, as did an Anthropic Message Batches job (`mode: job`, polled) end to end. The
Anthropic run caught one incompatibility, fixed in this release: newer Claude models reject
`temperature`, so the Anthropic adapter now retries such a call once without it.

Not yet run live: the cross-provider fallback with a real Anthropic candidate failing over to
OpenAI, and Anthropic JSON mode and tool calls. CI covers all three against the stub, and
`live-check.sh` runs them against the real APIs.

## Limitations, stated up front

- **An async held call still occupies the outbox's serial delivery** for its duration. Use a sync
  channel or `mode: job` when that matters.
- **A crash can cost a second call** if it lands after the model answered but before the result
  was recorded. Duplicate replies are deduplicated; the provider's bill is not.
- **Not yet:** token budgets and request-rate limits (only `concurrency`); IAM request signing for
  Bedrock; jobs for Bedrock and Gemini; callbacks routed through a message broker; sync calls on
  broadcast fan-out. The job table and the crash marker are PostgreSQL-only.
- A failed sync call without `<q:retry>` fails the instance instead of routing to a boundary.

## Upgrading

**Nothing to do** for a package that does not call a model. No package format or persistence schema
changed for existing channels: only an `ack-mode` declared explicitly on an outbound channel selects
the sync path, so existing channels keep their behaviour. Two deploy-time changes to be aware of:
`<q:alias>` is no longer required by the BPMN loader on a channel-call task — the lint requires it
only when the target channel is async (same `ALIAS_REQUIRED` code) — and an instance inside an
in-memory sync chain holds its `max-concurrent-instances` slot until the chain ends.

The engine image includes all three provider adapters (`llm-openai`, `llm-anthropic`,
`llm-bedrock` cargo features of `sutra-dist`); a custom build can select a subset.

## Install

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/startr-trade/sutra:0.5.0
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/startr-trade/sutra/main/scripts/install.sh | sh -s -- --version v0.5.0
```
